pages.description: Meet Savi Saluwadana, a software engineer in Sri Lanka interested in agentic systems and open-source development. Explore his focus and product architecture.
pages.intro: I’m a software and product engineer based in Sri Lanka, interested in agentic systems and open-source development. My work connects product workflows, software architecture, backend systems and the platforms that operate them.

blocks.text: I’m interested in clear domain boundaries, strong data models, reliable APIs and systems that remain understandable as products grow. The [architecture reference](/engineering/) connects those concerns to specific projects.

rows: Agentic systems and Model Context Protocol
Code contributions, bug fixes, documentation and developer tools. Explore my [public GitHub work](https://github.com/savisaluwadana).
My [platform and DevOps focus](/#platform-devops) covers Kubernetes, delivery pipelines, observability and developer platforms.

blocks.text: I’m interested in agents that use tools, retrieval and workflow state to help people complete real business and developer tasks. I want to explore systems where the model’s reasoning connects to reliable APIs, explicit permissions, useful evaluation and observable execution.

items: Tool-using agents and MCP interfaces that respect domain rules and the permissions of the person using them.
Durable workflow orchestration, retries and recovery for tasks that span multiple services or take time to complete.
Multi-agent collaboration with clear responsibilities, shared evidence and human review for consequential actions.
Retrieval-augmented generation, evidence provenance and agent evaluation that make results inspectable and useful.

blocks.text: My current product work includes [Pain Intelligence Lab](/products/pain-intelligence/), [Property Management OS](/products/property-os/) and [DevRelOS](/products/devrelos/). Their implemented boundaries are documented in the [agent and MCP architecture comparison](/engineering/#agent-access). The broader topics above describe my development interests.

I’m interested in contributing code, fixing bugs, reviewing design decisions and improving documentation in open-source projects. Cloud-native infrastructure, Go, Kubernetes, developer platforms and agent tooling are areas I want to contribute to.

I value clear APIs, reproducible setup instructions, architecture documentation and examples that help other developers understand and improve a system. My [GitHub profile](https://github.com/savisaluwadana) and the public repository links on [product pages](/products/) provide places to inspect my work.
For code, documentation or engineering collaboration, [get in touch](/contact.html).

pages.title: Software Architecture, Go APIs & MCP Systems | Savi Saluwadana
pages.heading: Software architecture across product workflows.
pages.label: Engineering / Architecture reference
pages.description: Explore Savi Saluwadana’s product architecture: Go APIs, MCP access boundaries, local-first HR workflows, tenancy and transactional operations, with project references.
pages.intro: A reference to the boundaries behind my product work: where authority lives, how clients access it, and what a workflow actually guarantees. Each comparison links to the relevant product architecture and current scope.

sections.title: AI agents and MCP access boundaries

blocks.text: Model Context Protocol gives an agent a tool interface. The useful architectural question is what happens behind that interface: which service authorizes the request, where reasoning runs, and whether an action needs approval.

rows: MCP calls the same authenticated Go HTTP API used by other clients. Domain rules and tenant permissions remain server-side; the MCP server has no direct database connection.
A Next.js dashboard, Go API and workers share PostgreSQL as the system of record. Provider adapters and evidence provenance support the workflow; consequential outreach passes through approval gates.
A React interface and Express/MongoDB application expose research tools to an MCP host. Semantic reasoning runs in the connected host, rather than direct model-provider calls from the application.

blocks.text: These are different boundaries. An agent tool does not imply unrestricted writes or an autonomous production workflow. Product scope notes describe the implemented tools, provider configuration and evidence requirements.

[Advance HRIS](/products/advance-hris/) combines a Next.js web application with a Wails/React desktop console, encrypted SQLite payloads and a sync queue. The Go API and cloud PostgreSQL database remain authoritative. The local-first boundary belongs to the desktop workflow.

[NexusPOS](/products/nexus-pos/) has an optional Electron desktop shell around the retail application. Desktop packaging alone does not establish an offline checkout engine. That distinction matters when evaluating a product for disconnected operations.
To assess a local-first system, identify the authoritative record, the queued work, and the conflict-resolution boundary. A local database or desktop executable answers only part of that question.

A SaaS interface and a tenant-isolated backend are separate architectural concerns. [Property Management OS](/products/property-os/) documents multi-tenant rental operations, role-based access and domain rules in its Go API. [Acme Accounting](/products/acme-accounting/) currently uses one company and one administrator identity per database.

[Academix](/products/academix/) has role-aware academic workflows and SaaS plan surfaces, while broader tenant-isolation and automated-billing work remain subject to its roadmap. The product labels should be read together with the current implementation boundaries.

The reference point is the server-side rule: who can read or change a record, which organization owns it, and which transaction maintains its integrity. A dashboard or plan selector does not establish those guarantees by itself.

sections.title: Bookings, recurring orders and payment workflows

rows: Property and booking workflows connect to PayHere payment callbacks and S3 media. Payment and storage integrations need deployment-specific configuration.
Next.js and PostgreSQL support food commerce and scheduled recurring delivery. Checkout and subscription baskets currently use cash on delivery; automatic recurring card charging is not implemented.
Matching and event procurement use a Next.js/PostgreSQL application. Payment evidence is submitted and reconciled manually in the current MVP.

blocks.text: A booking, a recurring order and a payment represent different state changes. Keeping those boundaries explicit makes the architecture easier to inspect and prevents a delivery schedule from being mistaken for automated billing.

sections.title: Read the source and current scope
